title: dialog-promptset-coverage-and-heuristics
body:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working explainer and checklist for chat prompt sets used during model onboarding and regression testing. Focus is on: coverage (user intent space + adversarial cases), systematic persona/system prompt choreography, tool-calling determinism, and layered safety scaffolds that are testable in CI.

High-level goals:
- Define a coverage matrix that maps user intents to prompt variants and expected behaviors (safe refusal, tool invocation, follow-up question, direct answer).
- Create heuristics for when system vs persona prompts should be mutated vs preserved across model swaps.
- Specify deterministic tool-calling prompts + canonical tool signatures to reduce false positives/negatives in functional tests.
- Provide scaffold templates for safety pre-checks and refusal phrasing that can be evaluated automatically.

Quick context/assumptions:
- Target models vary (Open-source 7B-70B family and internal quantized variants). We need prompts that are robust to temperature/beam changes and shorter context lengths.
- Our runtime supports structured function/tool calling (JSON signature) and streaming; tests should assert both content and call metadata.
- Onboarding evals will run against baseline model v1.14 and candidate during canary rollout. Regression flags when exact-match heuristics or quality metrics drop beyond thresholds documented in AM-4821.

Coverage matrix (draft):
- Core user intents: factual QA, code generation, editing, summarization, persona chat, tool-lookup, scheduling, transaction requests.
- Safety/adversarial axes: prompt injection, roleplay bypass, hallucinated-oracle (fake facts), chained requests (multi-step exfiltration), person-specific PII requests.
- Edge-format cases: extremely terse prompts ("help"), long context with conflicting instructions, multi-turn ambiguous clarifications.
- For each cell we create: 3 prompt variants (normal, ambiguous, adversarial), expected modality (answer/refuse/tool), automated check type (regex, JSON-schema, semantic-similarity threshold).

Persona vs system prompt choreography:
- Principle: system prompt establishes invariant constraints (safety, persona-agnostic policy). Persona prompt introduces style/role and optional task-specific heuristics (e.g., "You are an assistant that answers as a financial advisor — always use conservative language").
- Heuristics:
  - Keep safety rules strictly in system prompt; never move safety wording into persona. Reason: easier to verify once and avoid accidental overwrites in persona variations.
  - Persona prompts should be short (<= 2 sentences) and include explicit tool-calling hints when relevant (see tool-calling section).
  - When onboarding models, run a suite where persona is blank, persona=short, persona=long to detect sensitivity.

Tool-calling policy and canonical prompt signatures:
- We adopt explicit tool trigger templates to reduce spurious calls. Template: "If you need external data to answer, call TOOL_NAME with {json_schema}. Otherwise, respond."
- Example canonical call instruction (for retrieval tool):
  "If the answer requires fetching documents, call call_retrieval({"query": string, "top_k": integer}) and return only the fields 'id' and 'snippet'. Do not fabricate."
- Tests will assert: tool call name equality, presence and type-correctness of required fields, and that the assistant does not include tool output inline unless explicitly allowed.
- Heuristic for avoiding hallucinated calls: require presence of explicit confidence hedge in generation when model has low retrieval evidence (we check via LLM-simulated confidence and over-reliance regression).

Safety scaffolds (layered):
1) Input-level sanitizer: strip PII tokens based on regex whitelist and flag unusual request patterns (automation checks).
2) System-level refusal anchors: a short set of refusal templates and a refusing-structure that always includes 'I can't help with that' + 'if you need X, try Y' where X is allowed alternative. Keep templates in a testable file.
3) Persona-level guardrails: persona can provide helpful tone but cannot override system refusals. Tests include random persona overrides to ensure system wins.
4) Post-generation filter: lightweight classifiers that detect policy violations with tuned thresholds; flagged outputs go to safe-fallback route (summary refusal + human-review ticket).

Refusal phrasing examples (canonical):
- Direct illegal request: "I can't assist with that. If you need legal advice, consult a licensed attorney."
- Privacy/PII extraction: "I can't provide or extract personal data. If you have permission, please use the secure upload flow."
- Tool-protected data: "That information is only available via the connected database tool; I can call it if you provide the required consent token."

Regression test design:
- For each intent cell and prompt variant run against baseline and candidate models. Capture:
  - Response type label (answer/tool/refuse/clari) via automated classifier + manual spot checks.
  - Semantic similarity score to expected answer (embedding cosine cutoff).
  - Hallucination score (NER mismatch vs ground-truth KB for factual queries).
  - Tool-call exactness (name + payload match).
- Failure triggers:
  - Increase in hallucination rate > 3% absolute across a seedset of factual prompts.
  - Tool-call false positives > 2% or false negatives > 4% (we care more about missed calls for transactional flows).
  - Refusal tone regression: increase in terse/hostile refusals measured via sentiment model.

Practical prompt templates (examples):
- Summarization with tool hint:
  System: "You are a concise summarizer. Never invent facts. Use retrieval tool when unsure"
  User: "Summarize the following notes and call call_retrieval if you need sources: <notes>"

- Scheduling with deterministic tool call:
  System: "You may use calendar_tool({"date": string, "time": string, "attendees": [string]}) to create events."
  User: "Schedule a meeting next Tuesday 10am with Priya and Noah about "Q4 infra"."

Open questions / risks to address:
- How brittle are our tests to small wording changes in system prompts? We need to parameterize tolerances.
- Should we lock certain token sequences in system prompt to prevent downstream model rewriting? (tradeoff: reduces model flexibility).
- Tool-call schema drift: when we roll out new tool versions we need automated migration tests (ENGINF-237).
- How do we measure long-tail adversarial chains? Current seedsets don't cover multi-step exfiltration well. Propose to synthesize adversarial sequences via mutation fuzzer.

Immediate action items:
- [Evelyn] produce canonical refusal template file and check-in with legal for wording (due 2026-02-27). Linked: AM-4821.
- [Noah] implement unit tests for tool-call signature assertion in the runtime (PR referenced above). Due 2026-03-05.
- [Priya] expand the factual seedset with 500 more KB-linked prompts (focus healthcare & finance edge cases). Due 2026-03-12.
- [Team] run initial regression harness against quantized-13B candidate and capture delta report (bench with both temp=0.0 and temp=0.7).

Notes to self / informal thoughts:
- We should keep a short 'sanity seed' list that always runs in PRs (10 items) targeting the most critical tool flows: calendar, payments, retrieval, code-exec.
- Consider a separate 'persona-sensitivity' test that forces persona rewrites to attempt to contradict the system prompt and assert system dominance. Good litmus for prompt layering robustness.

References and related artifacts:
- See AM-4821 for onboarding threshold defs.
- See ENGINF-237 for runtime call assertion work.
- PR: runtime tool-call tests: https://github.com/redwood-inference/llm-runtime/pull/489

This doc is intentionally concise and operational — expand into a full PRD if the above items get accepted in the weekly applied-ml sync.
